title: Attacks on the Freedom of Assembly: Lessons from Digital Rights Defenders
content:
In 2026, two cases revealed how civic space is eroding, and those defending digital freedom and combating disinformation are on the frontline.

RightsCon, the world’s leading summit on human rights and technology, was due to be held in Lusaka, Zambia on May 5-8. Civil society, technologists, academics and policymakers were set to tackle some of the digital age’s most pressing issues: AI, surveillance, the militarisation of tech, disinformation, and online hate, among them.

But just days before the summit was going to open, and with more than 3,000 delegates about to arrive in Lusaka, the Zambian government unilaterally postponed the event because it did not align with “national values”. The decision, according to local reports, was made after Chinese diplomats pressured the Zambian government, objecting to the presence of Taiwanese civil society delegates at the conference.

In October, another attempt by a foreign power to intervene in a civil society gathering occurred.
